limitations: One engine-assisted reviewer. Ordinary root variations and played-move probes reviewed before neural rankings or extra-choice evidence. No consensus adjudication.

cases.rationale: The d-pawn and active king hold the rook pair in place. Rxd2+ Rxd2 and the c-pawn break show the immediate race.
Black reaches the same drawn rook ending by Ke5 or Rxa2. The king's route and active rook compensate for the loss of the passer.
Qxc3 is the precise defence. After Qe3, Qxd6+ followed by Rd2+ converts the attack into a forced exchange with a decisive material difference.
Bxg3 safely removes the passer. White's other plans must calculate the h-file and the knight's route through h5 and f4.
White's a-pawn and rook activity dominate. Black's different rook placements give up similar positional ground, with no clear forcing choice among them.
Kxf4 must deal with the bishop immediately. The later e-pawn loss changes rook activity. c4 leaves the bishop alive and allows a much stronger attack.
The rook checks hold the position while the d-pawn threatens promotion. Kh2 retains the checking resource even after d2.
Rxf1+ forces a rook exchange before the f7 pawn can advance. Moving to d7 allows a forcing sequence of queen and rook exchanges on f7.
The two opposing passers drive the position. Rb1 gains the required rook tempo and promotion can come with check, even after White queens first.
Re1+ forces the rook exchange and changes access to the d-pawn. White's rook placements determine which side can contain it afterwards.
A rook check or the immediate a-pawn advance can transpose. Both sides manage the passer and rook activity through several equal choices.
White's a-pawn ties the rook to the queenside. Black's d- and e-pawn counterplay and the Rxc2+ sequence require concrete calculation.
